title: Reference
text:
Core Panchanga entities
For a given Julian day number (jd) and place (latitude, longitude, timezone), compute:

tithi() / tithis() — lunar day
vaara() / vaaras() — weekday
nakshatra() / nakshatras() — constellation
yoga() / yogas() — yoga
karana() / karanas() — half-tithi

title: VedicDateTime
text:
Convert Gregorian dates (or Julian day numbers) into key Vedic calendar entities (Panchanga) in R.
VedicDateTime is an open-source framework that implements the Vedic calendar and provides conversions for Gregorian dates, motivated by analyses where both solar and lunar cycles matter (e.g., time-series seasonality and holiday effects).
Get started
Reference

title: VedicDateTime
text:
Highlights

Implements core Panchanga components and related entities:

Tithi (lunar day), Vaara (weekday), Nakshatra (constellation), Yoga, Karana (half-tithi)
Additional entities and helpers used in Vedic calendar computations

Converts from Gregorian date-time or Julian day number to Vedic entities
Designed to support research workflows, including time-series analysis

title: About
text:
VedicDateTime is an R package that implements the Vedic (lunisolar) calendar system and provides conversions from Gregorian dates (and/or Julian day numbers) to Vedic calendar entities.
It is intended to support research and applied workflows where lunar/solar cycles are relevant.

title: Articles
text:
Calendar systems can be solar, lunar, or lunisolar. The Vedic calendar is lunisolar, derived from the motions of both the sun and the moon, and can be useful when the phenomenon of interest depends on both.



The “five arms” of the Vedic calendar (Panchanga) commonly refer to:

Tithi
Vaara
Nakshatra
Yoga
Karana

title: Getting started
text:
Core concepts
VedicDateTime focuses on converting a Gregorian date-time (or Julian Day Number) to Vedic calendar entities.
Most computations require:

Time: Gregorian date-time (or already-computed Julian day)
Location: latitude, longitude
Timezone: often represented as UTC offset (e.g., 5.5)

title: Getting started
text:
Typical workflow

library(VedicDateTime)

# 1) Convert Gregorian date-time to Julian day number
# jd <- gregorian_to_jd("2023-10-24 12:00:00", tz = "UTC")

# 2) Define place (latitude, longitude, timezone)
# place <- list(latitude = 19.0760, longitude = 72.8777, timezone = 5.5)

# 3) Compute Panchanga entities
# tithi(jd, place)
# vaara(jd, place)
# nakshatra(jd, place)
# yoga(jd, place)
# karana(jd, place)

title: VedicDateTime website (GitHub Pages)
text:
This folder contains a Quarto website intended to be published with GitHub Pages.



Install Quarto: https://quarto.org/
In RStudio (or terminal), from this folder:

quarto preview



quarto render
This renders the site to docs/ (configured in _quarto.yml).



Recommended approach for a project site:

Commit the website source files and the generated docs/ folder to your default branch (e.g., main).
In GitHub repo → Settings → Pages:

Source: Deploy from a branch
Branch: main
Folder: /docs

Save. GitHub will publish at:

https://<OWNER>.github.io/<REPO>/






Choose a domain, e.g. vedicdatetime.example.com.
In GitHub repo → Settings → Pages → Custom domain:

Enter your domain and save.

DNS configuration (typical):

For a subdomain (vedicdatetime.example.com): create a CNAME record pointing to <OWNER>.github.io.
For an apex domain (example.com): use A records to GitHub Pages IPs (see GitHub docs).

Create docs/CNAME containing exactly your domain name on one line.

Start by copying CNAME.template → docs/CNAME and editing it.

(Recommended) Enable Enforce HTTPS in GitHub Pages settings after DNS propagates.





Set website.repo-url and the navbar GitHub link in _quarto.yml
Decide whether this is a project site (https://<OWNER>.github.io/<REPO>/) or user/org site (https://<OWNER>.github.io/)
Run quarto render and commit the generated docs/ folder
GitHub → Settings → Pages → Branch: main and folder /docs
Confirm all links work on the published URL





Update _quarto.yml with:

website.repo-url
